analysis.one_liner: Requires employer health plans to grant exceptions when 'try a cheaper drug first' rules would harm a patient.
analysis.headline: A bill to let patients bypass insurer 'fail first' drug rules drew 235 cosponsors from both parties — a majority of the House — but never got a vote.
analysis.plain_summary: Many employer health plans use "step therapy": before covering the drug your doctor prescribed, they require you to try one or more cheaper alternatives first. This bill would require those plans to set up a clear process for granting exceptions, in cases such as when the required drug already failed, is likely to cause harm, or when delay could cause severe or irreversible damage. Plans would generally have to answer within 72 hours, or within 24 hours when the delay could seriously jeopardize a patient's life or health.
analysis.who_benefits: Patients on employer-sponsored health plans whose doctors prescribe a drug the plan won't cover until cheaper options have been tried and failed. This includes people with autoimmune diseases, cancer, multiple sclerosis, and other conditions where trying the wrong drug first can mean months of pain, permanent damage, or lost ability to work. Patients who are already stable on a drug that worked under a previous plan would also be protected from being forced to switch.

how_it_helps.text: Plans must grant an exception when the required drug already failed, is expected to fail, could cause an adverse reaction or harm, would interfere with work or daily living, or when the patient is stable on a drug previously approved for them.
Plans must respond to routine exception requests within 72 hours, and within 24 hours when the step therapy protocol could seriously jeopardize the patient's life or health.
If an exception is granted, the plan must cover the drug at the cost-sharing rates the patient had when they enrolled, so they are not penalized for the plan's protocol.
Plans must post the exception process, required forms, and criteria publicly on their websites, so patients and doctors know the rules in advance.

analysis.who_pays: Employer health plans and the insurers that administer them bear the cost of reviewing exception requests and covering more expensive drugs sooner. Some of that cost would flow back to all enrollees through slightly higher premiums, since step therapy exists largely to hold drug spending down.
analysis.who_pays_short: Employers, insurers, and all plan enrollees

drawbacks.text: Step therapy is a cost-control tool: it steers patients to cheaper, often equally effective drugs first. An exceptions process weakens that tool, and the added drug spending is likely to show up partly in premiums paid by all employees.
The bill applies only to employer group plans under the Employee Retirement Income Security Act. People covered by individual marketplace plans, Medicare, or Medicaid get no protection from it.
The exception for patients already stable on a drug requires documentation of prior approval by another plan, which can mean extra paperwork and delay even in cases that seem straightforward.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For patients whose prescribed drug is medically necessary, the benefit is real and sometimes urgent — avoiding irreversible harm beats modest premium pressure. The bill is narrow and targeted rather than a ban on step therapy, which limits but also contains its cost. Its main design weakness is that it leaves most Americans with other coverage types out.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was referred to the House Education and the Workforce Committee the day it was introduced, and the committee never took it up before the Congress ended.

narrative.text: The bill was introduced on April 13, 2023 by Rep. Brad Wenstrup with a bipartisan group of original cosponsors and referred to the House Committee on Education and the Workforce.
It attracted 235 cosponsors — 154 of 216 House Democrats and 81 of 224 House Republicans — a majority of the full House.
No further action was ever recorded: the committee never marked up the bill and it never reached the House floor.
The 118th Congress ended on January 3, 2025, so the bill died without a vote and would have to be reintroduced to move again.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Employers and insurers keep step therapy without a mandated exceptions process, preserving their leverage over which drugs patients can get and when. Patients whose doctor-prescribed drug is blocked by a fail-first requirement gain nothing.

sides.party_line_note: Support was strongly bipartisan: 154 of 216 House Democrats and 81 of 224 House Republicans cosigned, so the bill had majority backing from both parties and died without opposition ever having to cast a vote.

industries.industry: Health insurers and employer plan administrators
industries.note: The bill forces them to grant exceptions to step therapy protocols they currently apply at their own discretion, covering costlier drugs sooner and running the review process on a clock. Their interest in unrestricted step therapy runs against patients who need the exception.
PBM-run utilization management, including step therapy, is a core tool for controlling drug spending. A mandatory exceptions process with 72-hour and 24-hour deadlines limits that control.
Fewer step-therapy barriers mean newer, more expensive drugs reach patients faster, boosting sales. Patients get quicker access, but the added drug spending feeds into premiums paid by all enrollees.
